messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Khan, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian man, has been working as a hotel manager for over three decades. His life took a dramatic turn after an incident involving toxic chemical exposure at his workplace. The event occurred during a routine maintenance operation when a pipe burst, releasing a noxious gas into the air. Mr. Khan was in the midst of it, and despite his best efforts to escape, he found himself overwhelmed by the smell and taste of the chemicals, which left him feeling both physically ill and deeply shaken. Since that day, Mr. Khan has been plagued by vivid memories of the event. Whenever these memories intrude upon his consciousness—often unbidden—he relives the terrifying moment as if it were happening again. The intense flavor of the chemical lingers in his mouth, a constant reminder of the fear and helplessness he felt during the incident. This helplessness has become one of Mr. Khan's most pressing concerns. He feels that he cannot prevent bad things from happening to him, leading to an overwhelming sense of vulnerability. This belief fuels much of his behavior: he constantly monitors his body for signs of danger or injury, checks his surroundings for any potential threats, and avoids situations where others might remind him of the traumatic event. Mr. Khan's constant scanning of his environment is not just a reaction but has become an ingrained habit. The more he scans and feels tense, the more convinced he becomes that he cannot trust his own body to keep him safe. He believes that his body’s heightened state of alertness is a sign that something bad could happen at any moment. The intrusive memories are particularly distressing for Mr. Khan because they remind him of how helpless he felt during the incident. When these memories force their way into his mind, he often reacts as if he were in immediate danger again. The memory of the taste of chemicals triggers a physical reaction that makes him feel like he is back in that moment of terror. This has led to an increase in false alarms, where he overreacts to benign situations. Mr. Khan’s work as a hotel manager is now complicated by his maladaptive strategies. He avoids certain areas of the building and steers clear of conversations about safety protocols or maintenance issues. His colleagues have noticed that he seems on edge much of the time, which has affected his ability to interact effectively with staff and guests. His relationship with his partner has also been strained. Mr. Khan often finds himself lashing out in frustration when things take longer than expected, interpreting delays as signs of impending doom. This heightened state of alertness and his constant scanning for threats have made it difficult for him to relax or feel at ease in any environment. He feels that he no longer belongs anywhere and struggles with a profound sense of isolation. The more Mr. Khan engages in these maladaptive strategies, the worse his symptoms become. When he scans his surroundings and constantly checks his body for signs of danger, the memories intrude even more frequently. The intrusive memories themselves reinforce his negative appraisals about helplessness and unreliability, creating a cycle that feels impossible to break. Mr. Khan has come to believe that seeking professional help is the only way out of this downward spiral. He is most afraid of never feeling safe again, but he also hopes for a return to a sense of normalcy where his fears don't control him so completely. The incident at work has left Mr. Khan with profound anxiety and a deep-seated belief that he can no longer trust himself or the world around him. He now seeks help to regain some semblance of peace and control over his life.
